## Charter

# CHARTER — Bridging the Interconnection Queue

## Deliverable
What: "Bridging the Interconnection Queue: State Policy Options for
Distributed Battery Storage, 2026-2030" — a policy research report.
Format: markdown, rendered last via the format skill (docx for state
legislative staff distribution).
Total size: 20000w

## Audience
State energy office policy directors and legislative committee staff who
already know what interconnection is but do not track battery-specific
queue data across states. They will skim the executive summary and read one
or two case studies closely; assume no prior exposure to Federal Order
2222-B.

## Voice & register
Third person, policy-analyst register — precise, unadorned, comfortable with
numbers. No first person, no rhetorical questions, no advocacy language;
present tradeoffs, not verdicts.

## Non-negotiables
1. Every statistic, dollar figure, or year carries a [S#] source tag traceable
   to a file in Sources of truth.
2. The terminology lock is followed exactly; no synonyms for locked terms.
3. Model legislation is always presented as an option among options, never as
   a recommendation the report insists a state adopt.
4. No section contains concluding or summarizing language except the
   Executive Summary and the Conclusion.
5. Case studies are presented as composites with tradeoffs stated, not as
   uncomplicated success stories.

## Terminology lock
- rooftop solar -> distributed solar
- battery storage -> battery energy storage system (BESS)
- utility -> distribution utility
- microgrid -> community microgrid
- ISO/RTO -> regional transmission organization (RTO)

## Out of scope
- Federal legislative process and any proposed changes to Federal Order
  2222-B itself.
- Wholesale electricity market design.
- Jurisdictions outside the United States.
- Net metering / retail rate design for exported energy (distinct policy

### sources/ferc-order-2222-summary.md

# Summary memo — Federal Order 2222-B (fictional)

Prepared by Cascadia Energy Policy Institute, Regulatory Affairs Desk.

Federal Order 2222-B (issued 2024, effective for RTO/ISO compliance filings
through 2026) requires each regional transmission organization to accept
aggregations of distributed energy resources — rooftop solar, behind-the-meter
batteries, and controllable water heaters — as a single dispatchable resource
in wholesale markets, provided the aggregator can demonstrate telemetry at the
device level. [S1]

Three consequences matter for state interconnection policy:

1. The order does not touch retail interconnection rules. States retain full
   authority over how a distribution utility processes an interconnection
   application, the queue in which it sits, and who pays for upgrades the
   application triggers. Federal Order 2222-B only governs what happens once
   a resource is already interconnected and wants to sell into wholesale
   markets.
2. Utilities report that 2222-B compliance filings have pulled engineering
   staff away from retail interconnection review, lengthening queues by an
   estimated 15% in the twelve months after a utility's compliance filing is
   accepted, though this figure is self-reported and not independently
   audited.
3. Aggregators now have a federal hook to demand faster retail
   interconnection, since a resource stuck in a retail queue cannot
   participate in the wholesale aggregation the order enables. This creates
   pressure states did not anticipate when 2222-B was issued.

Nothing in this memo should be read as a claim about wholesale market design;
that is out of scope for this report.

### sources/state-survey-2026.md

# 2026 Multi-State Interconnection Timeline Survey (fictional)

Cascadia Energy Policy Institute surveyed twenty-two state energy offices in
Q1 2026 on distributed battery storage interconnection practice. Eighteen
responded.

Key figures:

- Median time from application to permission-to-operate for a residential
  battery energy storage system (BESS) under 25 kW: 61 days (range 12-190
  days across responding states).
- Median time for a commercial BESS between 25 kW and 1 MW: 148 days (range
  40-310 days).
- Fourteen of eighteen responding states use some version of a "fast track"
  process modeled on the original 2013 interconnection procedures, but only
  six have updated the fast-track size threshold since 2020 to account for
  larger residential batteries entering the market.
- Nine states report a queue position deposit requirement; of those, five
  report the deposit is non-refundable if a customer withdraws after a
  utility has begun a supplemental review, which several state staff
  described as a deterrent to speculative applications but also a barrier
  for lower-income applicants.
- Twelve states report having no statutory deadline for a utility's
  interconnection decision at all; six have a deadline but no penalty
  provision if the utility misses it.

Respondent free-text comments (paraphrased, not directly quotable):
utility engineering capacity, not policy design, was the most commonly cited
bottleneck, mentioned by eleven of eighteen respondents.

### sources/utility-interconnection-timelines.md

# Utility-Reported Queue Data, Selected Utilities (fictional)

Data pulled from public interconnection dashboards maintained by three
investor-owned utilities and one municipal utility, Q4 2025 filings.

| Utility | Residential BESS median (days) | Commercial BESS median (days) | Active queue size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Verdant Power & Light | 44 | 132 | 3,102 |
| Highline Electric Cooperative | 71 | 165 | 640 |
| Basin Public Utility District | 58 | 140 | 1,215 |
| Norhaven Energy | 96 | 210 | 4,780 |

Norhaven Energy's queue grew 34% between Q4 2024 and Q4 2025, which Norhaven
attributes in its own filing to a surge in commercial BESS applications tied
to demand-charge management rather than to any change in its review process.

All four utilities report that supplemental review — triggered when an
application requires a distribution system impact study — adds a median of
90 additional days regardless of system size, and that supplemental review
is the single largest driver of queue time variance across applications.

### sources/case-studies-vermont-hawaii.md

# Case Study Notes: Two State Approaches (fictional)

## Vermont-style shared-savings queue reform

In this composite case, the state regulator authorized a "shared queue
priority" program in 2023: applicants who allow the utility to co-locate
their battery telemetry with a state-run monitoring platform move to the
front of the supplemental-review queue. Early results (18 months of data)
show program participants clearing supplemental review in a median of 51
days versus 90 days for non-participants, a $2,400 average avoided cost per
applicant in engineering re-review fees. Enrollment reached 61% of eligible
commercial applicants by month 18.

Tradeoff: the monitoring platform cost the state $3.1 million to build and
requires an ongoing $410,000 annual operating budget, funded through a small
per-application fee applied to all interconnection customers, participating
or not — a cross-subsidy some non-participants have objected to publicly.

## Hawaii-style capacity-mapping reform

In this composite case, the state required every distribution utility to
publish a public hosting-capacity map, updated quarterly, showing available
interconnection capacity by circuit. Applicants can self-screen before
filing. Utilities report a 22% reduction in withdrawn applications (fewer
customers filing where capacity was never available) and a 9% reduction in
median queue time for applications that do proceed, attributed to fewer
low-value engineering reviews of applications that would have failed anyway.

Tradeoff: two of four utilities in this composite required a rate case to
recover mapping-system costs, adding 14-20 months before the map went live.

### sources/cost-benefit-model-notes.md

# Cost Allocation Modeling Notes (fictional, methodology memo)

This memo documents the assumptions behind the cost-allocation comparisons
used in Section 5 of the report. It is a methodology note, not a source of
headline statistics — treat any figure here as illustrative unless it also
appears in state-survey-2026.md or utility-interconnection-timelines.md.

Three cost-allocation methods are modeled:

1. **Applicant-pays** — the applicant bears 100% of any distribution upgrade
   triggered by their interconnection. Simplest to administer; concentrates
   cost on whichever applicant happens to trigger a threshold upgrade,
   sometimes called the "but-for" or "cost-causer" problem.
2. **Socialized-through-rates** — upgrade costs are added to the utility's
   rate base and recovered from all ratepayers. Removes the but-for problem
   but weakens the price signal that tells applicants where capacity is
   scarce.
3. **Hybrid threshold** — applicant pays up to a fixed dollar threshold per
   kW of nameplate capacity; costs above the threshold are socialized. This
   is the approach modeled in most of the model legislation drafted for
   Section 5.1.

The illustrative modeling in this memo assumes a distribution upgrade cost of
$180,000 per substation-level constraint resolved, spread across an average
of 40 applicants under the hybrid threshold method versus 1 applicant under
applicant-pays. These are modeling assumptions for sensitivity testing only
and must not be cited in the report body as observed data.
